title: Pitkin County well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Pitkin County the median well depth is about 105 ft, with most completed wells between 60 and 210 ft in fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Water wells in Pitkin County, Colorado
intro_html:
Pitkin County wells are all mountain wells in fractured bedrock, serving homes and cabins from Aspen and Snowmass Village to Woody Creek and Redstone. The state has records for 4,760 well permits here, so we have a decent picture of how deep drillers usually go, what kind of production they hit, and what that means for cost on a new build or rural purchase.

Below is a plain-English breakdown of the depth, yield, water levels, drilling history, and risks you should think through before you buy land or plan a new well in this part of the Rockies.

sections.heading: How deep wells usually are in Pitkin County
sections.html:
Across Pitkin County, the median well depth is 105 feet. Half of the reported wells fall between 60 and 210 feet, which is the range most drillers will use to rough in a bid for a typical domestic well here.

About 47% of wells are under 100 feet, and another 37% run 100–300 feet, so shallow to mid-depth holes are common in this fractured bedrock. Deeper completions do show up: 14% are 300–600 feet and 2% are over 600 feet, with the deepest on record at 1,510 feet.

That spread tells you depth is site-specific. Two lots in the same valley can differ by hundreds of feet depending on fractures in the granite and gneiss.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Production in Pitkin County is generally solid for mountain wells. The median reported yield is 15 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells come in between 10 and 15 gpm. For a single home on an exempt household-use permit, that is plenty of capacity when paired with proper storage and pump controls.

The low end is a smaller slice here: only 1% of wells report under 1 gpm and 5% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. About 30% land in the 5–15 gpm range, while 64% report 15 gpm or more.

Those numbers are encouraging, but fractured-rock wells are still unpredictable, so you plan based on nearby well logs, not countywide averages.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they suggest about the water table
sections.html:
For wells that report it, the median static water level in Pitkin County is about 50 feet below ground, with the middle half between 24 and 116 feet. That’s the distance from the surface down to the resting water level in the well.

Looking at medians by decade, water levels have bounced around but do not show a simple straight-line decline. The median was 37 feet in the 1980s, dropped to 95 feet in the 1990s, came back shallower to 48 feet in the 2000s, then 67 feet in the 2010s, and 51 feet so far in the 2020s.

That kind of variability is common in fractured-bedrock systems, where individual fractures matter more than a single regional water table.

sections.heading: Who drills here and how the permit history looks
sections.html:
The state has records for 4,760 well permits in Pitkin County, with 2,416 recorded as constructed and 2,855 reporting a total depth. That’s a long drilling history spread across the county’s valleys and ridges.

Permitting picked up strongly from the 1960s through the 1990s. There were 16 permits in the 1950s, 237 in the 1960s, 504 in the 1970s, 601 in the 1980s, and a peak of 1,136 in the 1990s. Activity stayed strong with 782 permits in the 2000s, 452 in the 2010s, and 323 already in the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025.

Most records list unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. The busiest drillers in the logs are Shelton Drilling Corporation, Collins Drilling Co, and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Pitkin County
sections.html:
Pitkin County drilling is almost all in fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss. Typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 105-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $6,800–$10,500 before any equipment.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that depth generally runs in the ballpark of $12,800–$22,500. Deeper holes push those costs up foot by foot.

When budgeting a build near Aspen, Snowmass, Woody Creek, or Redstone, it’s smart to price both a median-depth scenario and a deeper contingency, based on actual nearby well reports.

sections.heading: Risks to look for: low yield, contamination, and site layout
sections.html:
Even with strong countywide yields, there is still some risk: 1% of reported wells make under 1 gpm and 5% sit between 1 and 5 gpm. Those can function with storage and careful management but change how you design plumbing and irrigation.

Pitkin County also has mapped environmental concerns within about 10 miles of various wells: 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 130 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your well is contaminated, but water testing for metals and PFAS is reasonable due diligence.

On small or steep lots, leave room for both a code-compliant septic system and safe well setbacks so you aren’t boxed in when it is time to build.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Pitkin County well
sections.html:
When you’re looking at a Pitkin County property, start with the well permit and driller’s log. Depth, yield, and static level are recorded on many of the 2,855 wells with known depths and 948 with reported yields, and 232 list static water levels.

For vacant land, pull logs from nearby wells in the same valley before you write an offer. They give you a better sense of whether you’re more likely to see a 60–210 foot completion or something much deeper.

Expect domestic or household-use permits on most parcels, since about 71% of wells in the county are domestic/household. If you need more water for irrigation or shared uses, talk with a water attorney or engineer early about your options.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Pitkin County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on state records, the median well depth in Pitkin County is about 105 feet, with half of reported wells between 60 and 210 feet. Around 47% of wells are under 100 feet and 37% are between 100 and 300 feet. A smaller share, about 14%, runs 300–600 feet and 2% are deeper than 600 feet, including one well down to 1,510 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Pitkin County wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported production is generally good. The median yield is 15 gallons per minute and the middle half of wells are between 10 and 15 gpm. Only about 1% of wells come in under 1 gpm and 5% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Roughly 30% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and about 64% report 15 gpm or more, which is strong for single-family use.

faq.q: What is the water table depth in Pitkin County?
faq.a: For wells that report it, the median static water level in Pitkin County is about 50 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half between 24 and 116 feet. By decade, median levels have ranged from 37 feet in the 1980s to 95 feet in the 1990s and around 51 feet so far in the 2020s. That variation reflects fractured-bedrock conditions more than a simple, flat water table.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Pitkin County, CO?
faq.a: In Pitkin County’s fractured mountain bedrock, typical drilling runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 105-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is around $6,800–$10,500. By the time you add casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete domestic well at that depth typically falls in the $12,800–$22,500 range, with deeper holes costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Pitkin County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The county has 16 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 130 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles of some wells. Those sites do not automatically mean your water is bad, but they are good reason to test for metals, PFAS, and basic potability before relying on a well for drinking water.
